column4: خَافِضَةٌ رَّافِعَةٌ names the Resurrection itself by the section's two opposed motions: it lowers and raises.
فِي جَنَّةٍ عَالِيَةٍ is the exact high-garden scene of 88:10 in another judgment tableau.
The same verse says God raised the sky and وَوَضَعَ the balance, joining the section's roots for raising and placing in a divinely ordered cosmos.
The earth is seen خَاشِعَةً, then rain makes it stir and swell; a visibly low, still earth rises by God's gift.
Iblis is told to descend, that arrogance has no place there, and to leave among the abased; self-height becomes imposed lowness.
God makes the unbelievers' word السُّفْلَىٰ and His own word الْعُلْيَا, stating the image's vertical reversal as a verdict.
God could have raised the man by His signs, but he clung to the earth; bestowed elevation and chosen lowness meet in one sentence.
Joseph raises his parents onto the throne while they fall in prostration, placing honor and bodily lowering together without confusing either.
Worldly ranks are contrasted with the Hereafter, which is أَكْبَرُ دَرَجَاتٍ; its greater degrees clarify the garden's granted elevation.
The final home is assigned to those who do not seek عُلُوًّا in the earth, directly opposing self-awarded height to received afterlife height.
الْعَذَابِ الْأَدْنَىٰ is set below الْعَذَابِ الْأَكْبَرِ, making the lesser warning and greatest final punishment explicit.
Pharaoh's أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلَىٰ is the extreme form of a human giving himself the height that belongs to God.
God's seizure of Pharaoh in punishment for the last and first offense supplies the immediate answer to his claim of being “highest” in 79:24.
أَسْتَكْبَرْتَ أَمْ كُنتَ مِنَ الْعَالِينَ places arrogant self-enlargement and being among “the high” side by side in God's question to Iblis.
عُلُوًّا كَبِيرًا combines the section's two secondary roots in Israel's foretold great self-exaltation and corruption.
The command to glorify رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَىٰ reserves true highestness for the Lord; 87:12 later answers refusal with the greatest fire.
النَّارَ الْكُبْرَىٰ is the other Quranic “greatest fire,” and its surah has already named God as the Most High in 87:1.
After disgrace in the nearer life, وَلَعَذَابُ الْآخِرَةِ أَكْبَرُ makes the greater afterlife punishment the upper term of the same scale.
وَلَعَذَابُ الْآخِرَةِ أَكْبَرُ generalizes the ruined garden owners' worldly punishment into the greater punishment beyond it.
يَرْفَعِ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا makes elevation God's response to believers who make room and rise when commanded.
God says He raised some people above others in degrees as a test, so worldly height is explicitly bestowed and accountable.
Whoever seeks honor is directed to God: good speech ascends and righteous action raises it, replacing self-exaltation with a Godward ascent.
تُعِزُّ مَن تَشَاءُ وَتُذِلُّ مَن تَشَاءُ assigns both honor and abasement to God's giving, the governing claim of the section.
Sky, earth, sun, moon, stars, mountains and creatures prostrate, and whoever God humiliates has none to honor him; cosmic lowering and human rank share one divine judgment.
وَرَفَعْنَاهُ مَكَانًا عَلِيًّا joins both elevation roots in Idris's God-given high station.
وَرَفَعْنَا لَكَ ذِكْرَكَ presents raised renown as God's gift, another non-spatial form of the section's bestowed height.
Believers who come with righteous deeds receive الدَّرَجَاتُ الْعُلَىٰ, making high ranks a judged reward rather than a self-claim.
The fruit clusters hang دَانِيَةٌ inside the high garden of 69:22, so what serves its honored people is brought low and near.
Garden shade is brought near and its fruit is made submissively low, matching the section's low service objects beneath honored occupants.
وَفُرُشٍ مَرْفُوعَةٍ repeats the scene of raised furnishings within the garden's reward.
اللَّهُ الَّذِي رَفَعَ السَّمَاوَاتِ directly attributes the visible height of the heavens to God's raising.
The next verse says He spread the earth and set mountains in it, completing 13:2's raised-sky/extended-earth frame that parallels 88:18–20.
رَفَعَ سَمْكَهَا describes God raising the sky's structure, a direct counterpart to 88:18.
وَالْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ دَحَاهَا completes the raised sky of 79:28 with the earth extended below.
وَالْأَرْضَ وَضَعَهَا لِلْأَنَامِ answers the raised sky of 55:7 with an earth laid down for creatures.
A mountain, the world's conspicuous height, would become خَاشِعًا and split from fear of God if it received the Quran.
The wrongdoers are shown before the Fire خَاشِعِينَ مِنَ الذُّلِّ, the same eschatological lowering of persons by humiliation.
خُشَّعًا أَبْصَارُهُمْ shows lowered eyes as people emerge from graves toward the caller on the Day.
خَاشِعَةً أَبْصَارُهُمْ تَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ exactly binds lowered eyes to the humiliation that overtakes them.
The promised Day is again marked by خَاشِعَةً أَبْصَارُهُمْ and enveloping humiliation, directly echoing the section's bowed faces.
أَبْصَارُهَا خَاشِعَةٌ gives the terrified resurrection scene the same downcast gaze.
The people of the garden have faces untouched by darkness or ذِلَّةٌ, the positive boundary opposite the humiliated faces of punishment.
For earners of evil, تَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ and darkened faces lead to the Fire, paralleling the section's lowered condemned faces.
The Day shows the faces of those who acted arrogantly blackened and names Hell as their lodging, joining self-height to facial abasement.
وَخَشَعَتِ الْأَصْوَاتُ lowers all voices before the Merciful in the resurrection gathering, extending bowed faces into bowed sound.
They fall on their chins weeping and revelation increases their خُشُوعًا, giving the root a voluntary bodily descent before God.
Those who arrogantly reject the signs find heaven's gates closed and the garden impossible to enter, a direct boundary between self-height and the high garden.
Those too arrogant to worship God will enter Hell دَاخِرِينَ, so their attempted height ends in abased entry.
Because people acted arrogantly on earth, they receive عَذَابَ الْهُونِ; earthly self-elevation is repaid as humiliating punishment.
عَذَابَ الْهُونِ is imposed for false claims about God and arrogance toward His signs, coupling greatness claimed with abasement received.
The arrogant are told to enter Hell's gates, making the punishment the settled destination of their self-enlargement.
Those who disdain and act arrogantly are promised painful punishment and no protecting ally, directly stating the consequence developed in the section.
ʿĀd act arrogantly and ask who is stronger than they, turning self-height into an explicit contest with their Creator.
The humiliating wind-punishment answers ʿĀd's boast in 41:15 and says the afterlife punishment is still more humiliating.
Pharaoh and his troops act arrogantly in the earth without right and suppose they will not return, the posture that precedes divine lowering.
God seizes Pharaoh and his troops and casts them into the sea, physically reversing the earthly arrogance named in 28:39.
The pride in disputants' breasts is مَا هُم بِبَالِغِيهِ, a self-imagined greatness they will never attain.
When admonished, the wrongdoer is seized by sinful pride; Hell suffices him, a concise nonlexical statement of self-height opening onto punishment.
Pharaoh orders Haman to build him a tower, turning his self-elevation into an attempted structure of ascent.
Pharaoh wants the tower's routes to reach the heavens, but the verse calls his scheme ruinous; fabricated ascent cannot reach divine height.
Pharaoh orders a baked-brick tower so he might look toward Moses's God, staging arrogant self-raising against the heaven God raised.
The swaggering person on earth is told he can neither split the earth nor reach the mountains in height, so creation itself limits self-importance.
God makes the overturned city's high part its low part, a literal punitive inversion of عَالِيَهَا and سَافِلَهَا.
The same destruction turns the city's عَالِيَهَا into سَافِلَهَا, making elevation collapse under judgment.
Those who sought to overcome Abraham are made الْأَسْفَلِينَ, a reversal from intended superiority to lowest position.
Hypocrites occupy الدَّرْكِ الْأَسْفَلِ of the Fire, the spatial opposite of the high garden.
Humanity is returned أَسْفَلَ سَافِلِينَ after the finest formation in 95:4, a sharp descent from granted stature.
Everything in the heavens and earth and the angels prostrate to God وَهُمْ لَا يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ; even elevated beings refuse self-height.
The prostrating beings fear their Lord مِن فَوْقِهِمْ and do what they are commanded, completing 16:49's vertical obedience.
Those who are “with Him” do not act arrogantly toward worship; true nearness and height produce service rather than self-enlargement.
The formerly arrogant tell the formerly weak that all are together in the Fire, where judgment erases their manufactured hierarchy.
Hardship is sent لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَضَرَّعُونَ, using the food-root's human sense for being brought low enough to implore God.
They fail to تَضَرَّعُوا when distress comes because their hearts harden, showing refusal of salutary lowering before punitive lowering.
Prophetic communities are seized by hardship لَعَلَّهُمْ يَضَّرَّعُونَ, another direct use of the named root for human abasement and appeal.
Punishment does not make them submit to their Lord and وَمَا يَتَضَرَّعُونَ, so their refusal to lower themselves persists.
God says He raised some people above others in degrees so they may employ one another in service, linking given rank with service rather than inherent worth.
نَرْفَعُ دَرَجَاتٍ مَّن نَّشَاءُ makes Abraham's argumentative rank an elevation God grants as He wills.
نَرْفَعُ دَرَجَاتٍ مَّن نَّشَاءُ frames Joseph's superior knowledge and plan as bestowed elevation.
God favors messengers differently and raises some in degrees, another explicit case of rank being conferred rather than seized.
وَأَنتُمُ الْأَعْلَوْنَ addresses believers after defeat with a conditioned, God-given upper standing rather than worldly boasting.
وَأَنتُمُ الْأَعْلَوْنَ assures believers of the upper position while God is with them, locating their height in divine accompaniment.
إِنَّكَ أَنتَ الْأَعْلَىٰ gives Moses the upper hand by divine assurance at the moment of fear.
The hypocrites claim the “mightier” will expel the “lowlier,” but the verse reserves true might for God, His messenger and believers.
Believers are أَذِلَّةٍ toward believers and أَعِزَّةٍ toward rejecters; chosen humility and principled strength replace a single social ladder.
وَاخْفِضْ لَهُمَا جَنَاحَ الذُّلِّ commands a merciful, voluntary lowering before parents, unlike abasement imposed by punishment.
أَنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ الْعَلِيُّ الْكَبِيرُ joins true height and greatness in God, setting the boundary for the section's warning about human self-greatness.
الْعَلِيُّ الْكَبِيرُ again belongs to God after false deities are declared false, defining legitimate elevation and greatness.
The heavenly intercession scene ends with وَهُوَ الْعَلِيُّ الْكَبِيرُ, reserving highness and greatness for the One above the fearful servants.
Judgment belongs to اللَّهِ الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ, الْعَلِيِّ الْكَبِيرِ; divine height and greatness stand over those who denied Him alone.
Pharaoh is described as لَعَالٍ فِي الْأَرْضِ and extravagant, a direct Quranic use of height for tyrannical self-exaltation.
إِنَّ فِرْعَوْنَ عَلَا فِي الْأَرْضِ immediately unfolds as division and oppression, defining the root's tyrannical secondary face.
Pharaoh's people deny signs ظُلْمًا وَعُلُوًّا despite inward certainty, locating “height” in willful domination.
Pharaoh is عَالِيًا among the transgressors, while 44:30 names Israel's rescue from his humiliating punishment.
لَقَدِ اسْتَكْبَرُوا فِي أَنفُسِهِمْ وَعَتَوْا عُتُوًّا كَبِيرًا gives self-enlargement and great insolence the section's exact secondary sense.
Those who arrogantly reject God's signs are companions of the Fire, stating the self-height/punishment sequence directly.
Qārūn, Pharaoh and Haman act arrogantly in the earth yet cannot outstrip God, denying their presumed height any escape.
Each arrogant party of 29:39 is then seized for its sin by storm, blast, sinking or drowning, supplying the differentiated lowering.
They respond to the command of divine unity with arrogance, identifying the stance that leads into the punishment announced nearby.
ذَائِقُو الْعَذَابِ الْأَلِيمِ gives the consequence of the arrogance named in 37:35.
ثُمَّ أَدْبَرَ وَاسْتَكْبَرَ marks the self-enlarging turn that precedes the threat of Saqar.
سَأُصْلِيهِ سَقَرَ supplies the fiery end of the arrogance in 74:23.
Rejecters are reminded that the signs were recited but they acted arrogantly and became criminals, immediately before their final exclusion.
The spending parable is جَنَّةٍ بِرَبْوَةٍ, a garden on elevated ground whose doubled yield makes height a received fertility rather than a social claim.
وَتَعَالَىٰ عَمَّا يَقُولُونَ عُلُوًّا كَبِيرًا uses the same “great elevation” language as 17:4 but reserves its true form for God's transcendence.
إِنَّ اللَّهَ كَانَ عَلِيًّا كَبِيرًا closes a warning against seeking advantage over another person, placing ultimate height and greatness with God.
الْكَبِيرُ الْمُتَعَالِ names God as the Great, supremely exalted One, the legitimate union of the two qualities humans counterfeit.
وَلَهُ الْكِبْرِيَاءُ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ assigns grandeur throughout the section's high-and-low cosmos to God alone.
الْمُتَكَبِّرُ appears as a divine name among God's names, marking the boundary between rightful divine greatness and blameworthy creaturely arrogance.
Pharaoh's sorcerers claim success will belong to whoever اسْتَعْلَىٰ, making competitive self-elevation the false premise that 20:68 overturns.
The sorcerers who sought the upper hand in 20:64 are cast down in prostration when truth appears, a bodily reversal that becomes faithful elevation.
Iblis refuses the commanded prostration and وَاسْتَكْبَرَ; unwillingness to lower himself is precisely his culpable self-height.
All the angels prostrate except Iblis, who acts arrogantly; the verse again stages chosen bodily lowering against self-enlargement.
أَنَا خَيْرٌ مِّنْهُ gives Iblis's self-ranking logic, which 7:13 answers with descent and inclusion among the abased.
The people stationed on the Heights tell recognizable men that their gathering and arrogance did not avail them, exposing claimed rank from an actual high vantage named in 7:46.
After gardens and fine dwellings are promised, وَرِضْوَانٌ مِّنَ اللَّهِ أَكْبَرُ gives “greater” a positive object beyond even elevated reward.
وَلَأَجْرُ الْآخِرَةِ أَكْبَرُ places the greater measure on afterlife reward, the positive counterpart to the section's greatest punishment.
God raises the mountain above the covenant people like a canopy and they think it will fall, making human lowliness visible beneath a divinely lifted height.
إِذَا وَقَعَتِ الْوَاقِعَةُ announces the event whose own action is specified as lowering and raising in 56:3.
The oath by السَّقْفِ الْمَرْفُوعِ presents the heaven as a raised roof, another expression of visible height made by God.
بَل رَّفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إِلَيْهِ makes Jesus's ascent explicitly God's act and therefore an instance of bestowed elevation.
God promises Jesus وَرَافِعُكَ إِلَيَّ, using physical elevation as a divine rescue and honor.
God permits certain houses أَن تُرْفَعَ and His name to be remembered there, joining elevation with worship rather than status-seeking.
رَفِيعُ الدَّرَجَاتِ ذُو الْعَرْشِ locates the possession of high degrees and the Throne in God before the warning of the meeting Day.
ابتِغَاءَ وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ الْأَعْلَىٰ makes the Most High Lord, not social height, the giver's sole object.
وَهُوَ الْعَلِيُّ الْعَظِيمُ reserves true exaltedness and immensity for the One whose Throne spans heaven and earth.
He owns what is in heaven and earth and is الْعَلِيُّ الْعَظِيمُ, grounding the section's vertical world in divine, not human, height.
The faithful are asked whether it is time for their hearts to تَخْشَعَ to God's remembrance, turning lowering inward before it appears on faces.
Successful believers are فِي صَلَاتِهِمْ خَاشِعُونَ, a chosen humility whose outcome contrasts with forced humiliation on the Day.
Prayer is called weighty except for الْخَاشِعِينَ, linking willing humility to the endurance that prevents later abasement.
People invoke God تَضَرُّعًا وَخُفْيَةً in the darkness of land and sea, using the named food-root's human sense of lowly entreaty.
ادْعُوا رَبَّكُمْ تَضَرُّعًا وَخُفْيَةً commands deliberate humble supplication, the constructive face of becoming low before God.
God is to be remembered تَضَرُّعًا وَخِيفَةً, making inward abasement a daily practice rather than an imposed final state.
وَاخْفِضْ جَنَاحَكَ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ commands the messenger to lower his wing to believers, a voluntary social lowering opposite pride.
وَاخْفِضْ جَنَاحَكَ similarly directs merciful lowering toward the believers who follow, giving honor through humility.
The garden's people recline on couches while the following verses lower shade and fruit and bring vessels to them, establishing the honored human position.
Silver vessels and cups are circulated among the reclining people, directly enacting the section's service-cup detail.
Golden dishes and cups are carried around the garden's people, so vessels serve rather than mark a low human rank.
The sincere servants sit عَلَىٰ سُرُرٍ facing one another, and 37:45 then brings a cup around to them.
A cup from a flowing spring is circulated among the people on couches in 37:44, matching the serving-vessel relation.
The God-fearing recline عَلَىٰ سُرُرٍ arranged in rows, while 52:23 has them pass a cup among themselves.
They pass a cup in the garden without idle or sinful speech, supplying the active service object beside the couches of 52:20.
The sky is built with power and made vast, while the next verse spreads the earth beneath it.
وَالْأَرْضَ فَرَشْنَاهَا completes 51:47's sky with an earth spread like a furnishing below.
God makes the earth a bed and the sky a building, a habitable above-and-below order close to the section's visible vertical world.
God makes the earth a settled place and the sky a structure, then fashions human forms well; the vertical order is explicitly His provision.
The audience is told to look at the sky above, how God built and adorned it; 50:7 turns next to the outspread earth.
The earth is extended and mountains cast into it beneath the sky of 50:6, paralleling the created sequence in 88:18–20.
Some faces on that Day are radiant, supplying the elevated side of the face-pair opposite humbled, darkened faces.
Other faces on that Day are grim, the corresponding condemned side of the eschatological face-pair.
Faces on that Day are bright, beginning another Quranic contrast between honored and abased human countenances.
Other faces on that Day bear dust, a visible lowering that 80:41 completes with darkness.
The Mount is raised above Israel as they take the covenant, an earlier occurrence of divinely lifted height over accountable people.
The Mount is again raised above Israel when their covenant is taken, repeating the same imposed vertical relation.
God raises the Mount above them for their covenant, joining physical elevation to commanded submission.
The purified scripture leaves are مَرْفُوعَةٍ, a non-spatial sacred elevation conferred on the reminder.
Pharaoh and his chiefs are قَوْمًا عَالِينَ, using the section's height root for an oppressive people's social self-exaltation.
Mary and Jesus are given refuge on a رَبْوَةٍ with secure rest and flowing water, another beneficent elevated place supplied by God.
